_notes: Notable-year highlights for the historical map slider's sidebar. Keyed by four-digit year as a string. THE `reviewed` FLAG IS A HARD GATE: map.html must refuse to render any entry where reviewed is not exactly true. That is deliberate belt-and-braces — Phase 1B's recommendation was that historical-accuracy stakes here are higher than the locomotive spotlight's, so an unreviewed blurb must not be able to reach the page through an oversight rather than a decision. The gate is enforced at load time (unreviewed entries are dropped from the in-memory map entirely, so no later code path can accidentally surface one) rather than at render time. NOT EVERY YEAR HAS AN ENTRY, and that is normal — the sidebar section collapses cleanly when the current slider year has no reviewed entry rather than showing an empty box. STUB SET ONLY: a small number of hand-verifiable entries so the rendering path can be exercised, plus one deliberately-unreviewed entry so the gate itself is testable. Generating these at scale is Phase 2C, using the approach in HISTORICAL-SLIDER-FINDINGS.md section 3 — derive candidate years statistically from the opening/closure series, have Claude draft from fetched text, and land them here with reviewed:false for human review.

_schema.year: four-digit year, also the object key
_schema.source: where the fact came from — 'wikipedia:{Article}' or a URL
_schema.reviewed: boolean. MUST be exactly true to render. Default false.

1825.blurb: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opens on 27 September — 25 miles of line, and the first locomotive-hauled public railway in the world.
1825.source: wikipedia:History of rail transport in Great Britain

1829.blurb: The Rainhill Trials are run from 6 to 14 October to settle what should haul trains on the nearly-finished Liverpool and Manchester Railway. Ten locomotives are entered, five compete, and Stephenson's Rocket wins — making the case for the steam locomotive over stationary winding engines.

1830.blurb: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens: the world's first inter-city passenger railway, and the first with scheduled services and terminal stations.
1830.source: wikipedia:History of rail transport in Great Britain

1836.blurb: The London and Greenwich Railway opens its first section — the capital's first steam railway, the first anywhere built specifically for passengers, and the first carried entirely on a viaduct.
1836._note: The line opened in stages between 1836 and 1838; the blurb says 'first section' rather than naming a completion date for that reason.

1837.blurb: The Grand Junction Railway opens, joining the Liverpool and Manchester Railway to Birmingham by way of Warrington, Crewe and Stafford. It is the first trunk railway completed in England.
1837._note: The source also calls it 'arguably the world's first long-distance railway with steam traction'. 'Arguably' is doing real work there, so the blurb claims only the first-trunk-railway-in-England point, which the source states flatly.

1838.blurb: The London and Birmingham Railway opens throughout on 17 September — 112 miles from Euston to Curzon Street, and the first inter-city line built into London.

1840.blurb: The Railway Regulation Act sets up the Board of Trade's Railways Department, forerunner of the Railway Inspectorate. No line may open without notice to the Board, companies must make returns, and government inspectors are appointed for the first time.

1841.blurb: Thomas Cook runs his first railway excursion, taking members of the Leicester Temperance Society to Loughborough — the start of organised rail tourism in Britain.

1844.blurb: Gladstone's Railway Regulation Act sets a minimum standard for rail travel, obliging companies to run cheap covered services for passengers who until then had ridden third class in open wagons — the 'Parliamentary train'.
1844._note: The Act is popularly remembered for the 'not more than one penny a mile' fare cap. That figure is NOT asserted here: it did not appear in the article text checked for this pass, and the rule is to source rather than infer. Worth adding if confirmed against the Act itself.

1845.blurb: Railway Mania is under way. The 1840s were by far the biggest decade of railway growth in Britain, peaking in 1846 when 263 Acts of Parliament authorised new companies.

1846.blurb: The Regulating the Gauge of Railways Act receives royal assent on 18 August, fixing 4 ft 8½ in as the standard gauge for Great Britain and 5 ft 3 in for Ireland.
1846.source: wikipedia:Regulating the Gauge of Railways Act 1846
1846._note: 1846 was also Railway Mania's zenith (263 Acts, 9,500 miles proposed) — but the existing reviewed 1845 entry already carries that fact, so this entry covers the Gauge Act only to avoid the slider saying the same thing twice.

1889.blurb: The Regulation of Railways Act. Passed within months of the Armagh rail disaster — in which a runaway excursion train killed around 80 people, many of them children — the Act made block signalling, the interlocking of points and signals, and continuous automatic brakes on passenger trains a legal requirement across Britain's railways. It's often regarded as the start of the modern era in UK rail safety.
1889.source: wikipedia:Regulation of Railways Act 1889; wikipedia:Armagh rail disaster
1889._note: DEATH TOLL IS DISPUTED BETWEEN SOURCES. Wikipedia's Armagh rail disaster article states plainly 'Eighty people were killed and 260 were injured, about a third of them children'; other accounts give 88 and a few give 89. 'around 80' is used deliberately so the sentence holds under the best-supported figure without asserting a precision the sources do not agree on. The Act's three provisions were checked directly against the Act's own article, which lists block signalling, interlocking of points and signals, and continuous automatic brakes (instantaneous, self-applying on loss of continuity, applicable to every vehicle, in daily use). SNAP POINT: 1889 replaced 1880 on 2026-08-04.

1923.blurb: The Grouping takes effect on 1 January. Over 120 companies are amalgamated into the Big Four — the GWR, LMS, LNER and Southern Railway — under the Railways Act 1921.

1938.blurb: PLACEHOLDER — NOT REVIEWED. This entry exists so the reviewed:false gate can be tested; it must never appear in the UI. If you can see this text on the site, the gate is broken.

1948.blurb: The Big Four are nationalised on 1 January under the Transport Act 1947, forming British Railways.

1963.blurb: The Reshaping of British Railways is published. It identifies 2,363 stations and 5,000 miles of line for closure — 55% of stations and 30% of route miles.

1994.blurb: Railway privatisation begins. Track and infrastructure pass to Railtrack while passenger services are franchised to private operators — originally 25 franchises.
1994.source: wikipedia:History of rail transport in Great Britain
